source: MIT 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics, Lecture 1, ~6-14 min
keypoints: A model is technically the description of any relationship between two or more variables.
Economics is a social science, not a real science: it has no rigid, universally applicable laws like those linking energy and mass in physics.
Models require simplifying assumptions that trade off two goals: explaining as much as possible versus keeping models parsimonious and teachable.
Two-good models give all the intuition needed for n-good models, just with easier math.
Statistician George Box wrote: all models are wrong, but some are useful.
The course teaches economics on three levels: mathematical, graphical, and intuitive, and success requires understanding all three.
Supply and demand was the first economic model, developed by Adam Smith in 1776 in The Wealth of Nations.
Smith's water-diamond paradox: water is essential for life yet nearly free, while diamonds are inessential yet very expensive.
The paradox is resolved by supply: the supply of water is vastly larger relative to demand than the supply of diamonds, which are rare.
The lecturer claims modern economics was born at MIT through the introduction of the tools of constrained optimization.
